power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≥ .118", "p = .302"), Sentence = c("The remaining comparisons -LARS -Productive, Interests, and Social, along with SMI -Behavior, SMI -Desire/Motivation, and KSADS-Depression -showed no significant mean difference between raters (all p ≥ .118).", "Spearman correlations, which index rank-order agreement independent of systematic mean differences, were generally weak-to-moderate and broadly tracked the ICC pattern (ρ = -.11 to .56), with the strongest rank agreement for SMI -Behavior (ρ = .56, p < .001) and the weakest for LARS -Interests (ρ = -.11, p = .302)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. facing greater risks for depression and adverse mental health outcomes than the general population of youth.

The psychometric properties of most measures remain untested with autistic youth even though autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity including unique cognitive, affective, behavioral and sensory needs.

The present study tested the internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, convergent and discriminant validity, and cross-informant agreement between 101 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) and their parents for several depression and social-emotional functioning measures (e.g., social motivation, anhedonia/apathy).
Most measures showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across informants, while confirmatory factor analyses yielded mixed evidence of structural validity.
Convergent validity was moderate and adolescent and parent reports agreed poorly to moderately, which emphasizes the value of collecting both perspectives.
Findings inform clinical practice by supporting the continued use of several measures in autistic adolescents, while suggesting caution in interpreting others.

Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. (1 in 31 8-year-old children diagnosed with autism 1 ) facing significantly greater risks for depression 2 , anxiety 3 , and suicidal thoughts and behaviors 4 compared to the general population of youth.
text.formatted: Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. (1 in 31 8-year-old children diagnosed with autism 1 ) facing significantly greater risks for depression 2 , anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">3</ref> , and suicidal thoughts and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref> compared to the general population of youth.

text.text: Despite these alarming statistics, few assessments and treatments exist to prevent and address adverse mental health outcomes in autistic youth. 2, 5, 6 Reliable and valid assessments are not only essential to screening and prevention efforts and diagnostic conceptualizations, but also to clinical trial readiness and accurate treatment planning. 7 Most assessments of clinical outcomes (e.g., depression, anxiety) and risk/protective factors (e.g., reward responsivity, social relationships) were developed for the general population, often excluding autistic youth. 8, 9 In fact, many assessments have not been validated for autistic youth and may not account for their unique neurodevelopmental differences and needs.

text.text: Efforts to establish the psychometric properties of assessments with autistic youth are necessary to understand and treat adverse mental health outcomes in this population.

Autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity 10 including unique cognitive (e.g., concrete thinking 11 ), affective (e.g., alexithymia 12 ), behavioral (e.g., routines, repetitive behaviors 13 ), and sensory needs, 14 which underscores the importance of establishing the psychometric properties of assessments with this population.
text.formatted: Autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10</ref> including unique cognitive (e.g., concrete thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11</ref> ), affective (e.g., alexithymia <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12</ref> ), behavioral (e.g., routines, repetitive behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13</ref> ), and sensory needs, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14</ref> which underscores the importance of establishing the psychometric properties of assessments with this population.

text.text: A key challenge facing mental health professionals is a limited evidence base on the rigor of assessments for autistic people, including: (a) whether generic assessments are reliable and valid, (b) if autism-adapted versions of assessments are more appropriate than generic ones, and/or (c) whether new assessments created for and with autistic people outperform generic assessments.

Initial findings indicate that some assessments developed for the general population (e.g., Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale; RCADS 15 ) are reliable and valid for use with autistic people. 16, 17 However, other findings suggest that autism-adapted versions of generic assessments 18, 19 increase their utility (e.g., Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale; C-SSRS 20 ) for the autistic community.

text.text: Similarly, some researchers advocate for creating new assessments (e.g., Suicidal Behaviours Questionnaire-Autism Spectrum Conditions; SBC-ASC 21 ) through community-based participatory research methods that not only capture the unique experiences of autistic people, but also cater to their neurodevelopmental needs.

text.text: As autistic people continue to experience adverse mental health challenges with little assessment and treatment options, efforts to increase the rigor of assessments are a critical starting point.

Semi-structured clinical interviews and questionnaires are common assessment approaches in research and clinical settings for the general population, with a limited evidence base for the autistic community.

For autistic people with social communication and interaction differences 14 , interviews may not be an optimal approach as they are perceived as confusing, stressful, ambiguous, and/or frustrating. 22 In one study, an adapted semistructured interview that accounted for the unique neurodevelopmental needs of autistic people (i.e., PARS-ASD 19 ) was more reliable and valid in assessing for anxiety symptoms and severity in this population than the generic version (i.e., PARS).

text.text: In another study, a generic interview (e.g., C-SSRS) reliably detected neurotypical youth at-risk for suicide, yet failed to detect 1 in 5 autistic youth at risk. 18 Importantly, the addition of a self-report questionnaire to the suicide interview increased the rigor of these screening efforts for autistic youth. 18 Initial findings suggest that some generic interviews may fail to capture the needs of autistic people, even though these interviews are widely used in clinical and research settings.

text.text: In another example, the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS 23 ) is a common interview of psychiatric symptoms and severity in youth that has had limited psychometric evaluation among autistic youth, representing a gap in assessment knowledge.

text.text: Parent report is another common assessment approach for identifying and treating mental health needs in youth. 24, 25 Parent-child rating discrepancies are common, 26 yet more salient for autistic youth and their parents than neurotypical youth and their parents. 27, 28 In one study, parent-child rating discrepancies were more significant among autistic child-parent dyads than neurotypical child-parent dyads on a common, generic questionnaire of depression (i.e., Children's Depression Inventory; CDI 29 ). 27 Depression is an internalizing condition that may be more challenging for parents to identify and report than externalizing conditions for which parent-child discrepancies are fewer 30, 31 ; additional research in this area is needed to clarify potential rating patterns.

text.text: Some investigators question the validity of generic self-report questionnaires among autistic youth 32 and advocate for stronger consideration of parent/collateral report, while other investigators highlight the importance of both youth self-report and parent report as raters may capture different, but equally important, information. 33, 34 Additional research on parent-child rating patterns is essential for improving the rigor of assessments for the autistic community as parents play a central role in youth access and engagement in treatment.

text.text: The present study aimed to test the psychometric properties of several generic interviews and questionnaires of depression, social motivation, and anhedonia/apathy with autistic adolescents and their parents.
The study aims were to test the psychometric properties of generic interviews and questionnaires including reliability, validity, and level of agreement between raters.

Given previous research, it was hypothesized that some assessments (e.g., RCADS 15 ) would be reliable and valid for autistic adolescents; for other assessments (e.g., K-SADS), reliability and validity would be tested for the first time in this population.
text.formatted: Given previous research, it was hypothesized that some assessments (e.g., RCADS <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> ) would be reliable and valid for autistic adolescents; for other assessments (e.g., K-SADS), reliability and validity would be tested for the first time in this population.

text.text: As rating discrepancies are more common for autistic parent-child dyads than neurotypical dyads, it was hypothesized that rating discrepancies would emerge across most assessments, to varying degrees.
Autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) without intellectual disability and one of their parents were recruited from the community through flyering and social media advertising.

Inclusion criteria included adolescents with: (a) an autism diagnosis, confirmed by record review of autism evaluations within the past 24 months [i.e., Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2 35 ) was administered] or ADOS-2 administration in lab, (b) without intellectual disability (IQ≥70), confirmed by record review of cognitive evaluations within the past 24 months (e.g., scores provided from Wechsler Scales of Intelligence) or administration of the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence, Second Edition (WASI-II 36 ) in lab.

text.text: Exclusion criteria included adolescents with: (a) severe aggression to self/others that compromise safety during study visits, (b) neurological disorders, (c) uncontrolled seizure disorder, and/or (d) intellectual disability (IQ<70).

text.text: Additional details regarding participant recruitment, screening, and eligibility are provided in our published study protocol [masked for review].
In this longitudinal study, families participated in four study visits over a one-year period; in the present study, data collected at the first study visit were analyzed.
In the first study visit, families participated in informed consent/assent, clinical interviews, neuropsychological testing, and surveys with adolescents and parents interviewed separately.
Families were financially compensated for their participation in study visits and could request a free psychological assessment report.

Informed consent and assent were collected in writing and all study procedures were approved by the [masked for review] Institutional Review Board (Protocol #22-00278) in accordance with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments.
Details regarding specific study procedures are provided in our published study protocol [masked for review].
Clinical interviews and questionnaires were completed by adolescents and parents separately.

Adolescents and parents completed the same interviews and questionnaires, apart from the Anticipatory and Consummatory Interpersonal Pleasure Scale (ACIPS 37 ) and Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA 38 ) which were only completed by adolescents.

text.text: Adaptive functioning and autistic traits.
Adaptive functioning was assessed by parent ratings on the Adaptive Behavior Assessment System, Third Edition (ABAS-3) 39 .

text.text: Autistic traits were assessed by parent-report in early development [Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ) 40 ] and the past six months [Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2) 41 ], and from adolescent perspectives [Comprehensive Autistic Trait Inventory (CATI) 42 ].

text.text: Adolescent social motivation was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the Social Motivation Interview (SMI) 43 , and a questionnaire, the Anticipatory and Consummatory Interpersonal Pleasure Scale (ACIPS) 37 .
text.formatted: Adolescent social motivation was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the Social Motivation Interview (SMI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">43</ref> , and a questionnaire, the Anticipatory and Consummatory Interpersonal Pleasure Scale (ACIPS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37</ref> .

text.text: The SMI is a semi-structured interview measuring levels of social motivation (i.e., interest/desire to engage with others and accompanying behaviors) in autistic youth (8-17 years old).
The SMI contains 23 items assessing youth social interest/desire and behaviors, each rated on a 4-point Likert-type scale with higher scores indicating higher social motivation.
Items comprise two subscales of social wanting and social behavior, which are summed into a total social motivation score.

Previous pilot testing of the SMI with 18 autistic youth suggested its feasibility of administration, user satisfaction, and promising psychometric properties 43 ; however, the authors noted a need for future examination of the SMI in larger samples.

text.text: The original 23 items of the SMI were administered in the present study, with additional questions added by our research team to more thoroughly examine and delineate social desire, behaviors, and outcome, with author permission.

This expanded SMI resulted in 18 items across three categories of social motivation (54 items total): (a) social desire/interest (e.g., degree of importance of a social situation, interaction, or relationship to the youth), (b) social behaviors (e.g., frequency and type of social behavior done by the youth), and (c) social outcome (e.g., degree of perceived success of a social behavior).
In the present study, items in each of the three categories were summed and compared in analyses as individual subscales without a total score.
The ACIPS is a 17-item questionnaire assessing reward capacity for social and interpersonal pleasure.
Items are rated on a 6-point Likert-type scale and summed into a total score, with higher scores indicating higher social motivation and reward.

In the adolescent validation study, the ACIPS was tested in 449 community adolescents aged 13-19 and showed excellent internal consistency (ordinal α = 0.95). 44 ACIPS scores correlated positively with TEPS anticipatory (r = 0.44) and consummatory (r = 0.30) subscales, supporting convergent validity, and were not significantly associated with general psychological distress (GHQ-12), supporting discriminant validity. 44 There is limited data on the psychometric properties of the ACIPS with autistic people.

text.text: In a sample of 49 autistic adults, the ACIPS total score demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .95) 45 ; however, its psychometric properties have not been tested with autistic adolescents.

text.text: Adolescent anhedonia/apathy was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the Lille Apathy Rating Scale (LARS) 46 , and a questionnaire, the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) 38 .
text.formatted: Adolescent anhedonia/apathy was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the Lille Apathy Rating Scale (LARS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">46</ref> , and a questionnaire, the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">38</ref> .

text.text: The LARS is a semi-structured interview measuring the presence and severity of apathy with items rated on a dichotomous scale.

The LARS is comprised of 33 items divided into nine domains (i.e., everyday productivity, interests, taking initiative, novelty seeking, motivation -voluntary actions, emotional responses, concern, social life, and self-awareness) that are summed into a total score of apathy, with higher scores indicating higher apathy.

In the founding paper, the LARS was tested in 159 patients with Parkinson's disease and 58 healthy controls, and showed high internal consistency (between-items α = 0.80, between-subscales α = 0.74) and strong test-retest reliability (r = 0.95), along with excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC = 0.98). 47 LARS scores correlated strongly with the Marin Apathy Scale (r = 0.87), supporting convergent validity, and reliably distinguished apathy from depression using an empirically derived cutoff (accuracy = 0.91, sensitivity = 0.89, specificity = 0.92). 47 The LARS has not been evaluated for use with autistic youth, which is a secondary aim of the present study.

text.text: The ASA is a 14-item questionnaire assessing general anhedonia in adolescents aged 11-18 years old.

Items are rated on a 4-point Likert-type scale and divided into three subscales (i.e., enjoyment, excitement, and emotional flattening; enthusiasm, connection, and purpose; and effort, motivation, and drive), which are summed into a total anhedonia score with higher scores indicating higher anhedonia.

The ASA was developed through qualitative interviews, then tested for structural validity using exploratory factor analysis in 1,057 adolescents and confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample of 1,041 adolescents; all adolescents were community/general-population adolescents. 38 The scale showed high internal consistency (total α = .93-.94 across samples) and good test-retest reliability over 7-11 weeks (ICC = 0.73). 38 ASA scores correlated strongly with depression (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire, r = .78) and negative symptoms of schizophrenia (Self-Evaluation of Negative Symptoms scale, r = .71), and more weakly with anxiety (RCADS subscales, r = .48-.52) and trait-level measures of behavioral approach/inhibition (r = .13-.40), supporting convergent and discriminant validity. 38 The ASA has not been evaluated for use with autistic youth, which is a secondary aim of the present study.

text.text: Depression.

Adolescent depression was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the modified depression module of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS) 23 , and a questionnaire, the Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS-47) 15 .
text.formatted: Adolescent depression was assessed using multiple units of analysis including an interview, the modified depression module of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">23</ref> , and a questionnaire, the Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS-47) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> .

text.text: The modified depression module of the K-SADS is a semi-structured interview used to assess the presence and severity of depressive symptoms in youth including depressed mood, irritability and anger, negative self-image, fatigue or lack of energy, concentration difficulties, psychomotor agitation, insomnia, anorexia, weight loss, and suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
Depression symptoms are rated on a 6-point Likert-type scale on the K-SADS, with higher scores indicating higher symptom severity.
The K-SADS demonstrated strong reliability in its initial validation study among non-autistic children and adolescents ages 7-17, including 55 psychiatric outpatients and 11 healthy controls.

Interrater agreement ranged from 93% to 100%, while test-retest reliability was strong across diagnoses, with κ values ranging from 0.63 to 1.00. 23 As noted, the K-SADS has limited psychometric evaluation with autistic youth, which is a primary aim of the present study.

text.text: The RCADS 15 is a 47-item rating scale of internalizing symptoms in youth completed by youth and their parents.
text.formatted: The RCADS <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> is a 47-item rating scale of internalizing symptoms in youth completed by youth and their parents.

text.text: All items are summed into a total score of internalizing symptoms, which is comprised of the following subscales: separation anxiety, generalized anxiety, panic, social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive traits, and depression.

In de Ross et al.'s (2002) psychometric investigation with 405 community Australian youth aged 8-18, the RCADS showed excellent internal consistency for the total scale (α = 0.96) and adequate-to-good consistency across subscales (α = 0.79-0.88), and confirmatory factor analysis supported the original six-factor structure (CFI = 0.83, RMSEA = 0.06). 48 Convergent validity was supported by moderate-to-strong correlations with the Revised Children's Manifest Anxiety Scale (r = 0.62-0.75) and with the Children's Depression Inventory for the Major Depressive Disorder subscale (r = 0.80). 48 The RCADS has been previously validated for use with autistic youth. 16, 17 In Kim and Lecavalier's (2024) study of 55 autistic youth aged 8-17 presenting with depressive or anxiety symptoms, the RCADS Total score showed excellent internal consistency at both administrations (α = 0.93 and 0.94), with major depressive disorder (MDD) subscale alphas ranging from 0.75 to 0.78. 49 Test-retest reliability over a two-week interval was good for most subscales (ICC = 0.74-0.87), with the MDD (ICC = 0.81) subscale showing high stability. 49 In the present study, only the RCADS depression subscale is presented and evaluated (a 10-item rating scale on a 4-point Likert-type scale).

text.text: Demographics and baseline adaptive functioning and autism-trait scores were summarized as median (Q1, Q3) for continuous variables and as n (%) for categorical variables.
All analyses were conducted in R version 4.6.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing), using the psych, lavaan, semTools, and correlation packages.

Two levels of analysis were used throughout: item-level analyses (internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis) were fit directly on raw item responses, while composite-score analyses (convergent/discriminant validity, cross-informant agreement) used the subscale/total scores described above.
Missing data were handled using instrument-specific rules for composite-level analyses.

For the ASA, following the guidance in the published scoring materials, the subscale scores and total score were prorated when 25% or fewer of items were missing; otherwise, scores were set to missing. 38 For the LARS and SMI, as no official guidance on missing items exists in the published scoring materials, a 25% missingness threshold was applied, consistent with the ASA.

text.text: For the LARS, the total score was in turn set to missing if any subscale was missing.

The K-SADS-PL likewise has no official guidance on missing items; given the absence of an established convention and only nine items in the instrument, any missing item resulted in the total score being set to missing.

The ACIPS was scored following the procedure used in its original validation study, in which surveys missing more than 10% of items were excluded from analysis and the remainder prorated. 44 The RCADS-47 was scored according to its manual scoring guidance, which recommends that subscales be prorated (summing completed items, dividing by the number completed, and multiplying by the total items in the subscale) when two or fewer items are missing, and left unscored otherwise; in our dataset, only the major depression subscale from this procedure was retained for analysis. 15 As a result, item-level and composite-level analyses can retain different effective samples, as detailed below.

text.text: Cases with any missing item within a given model were excluded listwise.
For measures with a subscale structure, firstorder factors were specified for each subscale, with items as indicators.
For LARS and ASA, subscale factors were further specified to load onto a single second-order general factor, consistent with the total scores computed for these instruments.
SMI subscales (behavior, desire, outcome) were modeled as correlated first-order factors without a superordinate general factor, as no SMI total score is calculated.
ACIPS, and the depression subscales of the KSADS and RCADS, were each specified as unidimensional single-factor models, consistent with their scoring as a single total.

Convergent and discriminant validity were evaluated by correlating (Spearman's ρ) composite scores across all six measures within each rater (adolescent, parent), based on an a priori set of same-construct ("convergent") pairs -SMI subscales with ACIPS, LARS with ASA, and K-SADS with RCADS depressionagainst all remaining cross-construct ("discriminant") pairs.

Pairs between two subscales of the same instrument (i.e., the three pairings among the SMI Behavior/Desire/Outcome subscales as SMI has no single total score) are neither convergent nor genuinely cross-construct and were therefore excluded from both groups.

Agreement between adolescent self-report and parent-report was evaluated, for every scale/subscale with both rater versions, using the two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, single-rater intraclass correlation ICC(2,1) 55 , the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired, non-parametric) to test for systematic mean differences between raters, and Bland-Altman 56 plots to visualize the pattern of agreement across the range of scores.

The sample included 101 adolescents (median age = 15.0 years, Q1, Q3 [14.0, 16.0]; 68.3% male, 31.7% female) and their parents (median age = 48.0 years, Q1, Q3 [45.0, 51.5]; 84.2% female).
The sample was predominantly White (64.5% of adolescents, 72.2% of parents), with 26.0% of adolescents and 30.5% of parents identifying as Hispanic/Latino.
Most parents held a college degree or higher (73.7%), and family income was distributed across the <$75,000 (22.4%), $75,000-$150,000 (41.2%), and $150,000+ (36.5%) brackets.

text.text: Across most scales, Cronbach's α ranged from acceptable to good (.71-.92), with generally comparable reliability between adolescent-and parentreport versions of the same measure.

The SMI subscales showed acceptable-to-good reliability for both raters (adolescent α = .76-.80; parent α = .80-.87), and omega-hierarchical and omega-total values were fairly close within each subscale, consistent with each SMI subscale functioning as an essentially unidimensional construct.
The ACIPS (α = .89) and the ASA subscales (α = .75-.89) showed acceptable-to-good adolescent-report reliability; parent-report versions are not available.

The LARS total score showed acceptable reliability for both raters (adolescent α = .76; parent α = .79); however, ω-hierarchical and ω-total diverged more substantially than for the other multidimensional totals, most notably for parent-report LARS, where ω-hierarchical (.38) was far lower than ω-total (.87), indicating that most of the reliable variance in parent-rated LARS total scores is attributable to the nine domain-level factors rather than a single general apathy factor.
A similar, but smaller divergence was present for adolescent-report LARS (ω-hierarchical = .40 vs. ω-total = .85).

The ASA total score showed a much smaller gap between the two (ω-hierarchical = .79 vs. ω-total = .94), suggesting its general factor accounts for more of the total score's reliable variance than LARS's does.
KSADS-Depression (α = .78 adolescent, .71 parent) and RCADS-Depression (α = .86 adolescent, .84 parent) both showed acceptable-togood reliability across adolescents and parents.

text.text: SMI fit poorly on every index for both raters (adolescents and parents), with CFI as low as .45 for adolescents.

ACIPS (adolescent-report only) showed acceptable CFI/TLI (~.90), but RMSEA (.11) and SRMR (.10) both landed just outside the acceptable range; however, RMSEA can artificially inflate in models with small sample sizes.
LARS showed the opposite split: RMSEA looked good for both raters (.06), but CFI, TLI, and SRMR (SRMR = .17, more than double the acceptable cutoff) all pointed to poor fit.
ASA (adolescent-report only) was the one model with no disagreement among indices -fit was good to excellent across the board, including a perfect CFI/TLI of 1.00.
KSADS-Depression fit well for adolescents but poorly across every index for parents.
RCADS-Depression showed the same pattern as ACIPS: solid CFI/TLI for both raters, but RMSEA (~.11) and SRMR (~.09-.10) both outside the acceptable range for both raters.
Convergent and discriminant validity, evaluated via Spearman correlations among composite scores within each rater, are shown in Figure 1.

text.text: Among adolescent report, the five a priori convergent pairs showed a higher mean correlation (mean ρ = .41) than the 20 cross-construct discriminant pairs (mean ρ = .25; three sameinstrument SMI subscale pairs were excluded from both groups).
Individually, all three SMI subscales correlated positively with ACIPS-Total as hypothesized (ρ = .33-.48), and KSADS-Depression correlated with RCADS-Depression (ρ = .62).
The LARS-ASA convergent pair showed a smaller positive correlation (ρ = .25) than the other convergent pairs.
Among the discriminant pairs, LARS-Total correlated negatively with ACIPS-Total (ρ = -.60); ASA-Total correlated positively with both RCADS-Depression (ρ = .72) and KSADS-Depression (ρ = .51).

Among parent report, where ACIPS and ASA are unavailable, leaving only the KSADS-RCADS pair as a convergent comparison, the single convergent correlation (ρ = .61) exceeded the mean of the 11 discriminant pairs (mean ρ = .23), though this comparison rests on a single correlation and should be interpreted accordingly.

text.text: The present study is among the first to test the psychometric properties of several interviews and questionnaires of mental health outcomes and risk/protective factors (e.g., depression, social relationships) in a modest sample of autistic adolescents and their parents.

Internal consistency estimates ranged from acceptable to good across most assessments, with generally comparable reliability between adolescent-and parent-report versions of the same assessment; findings provide preliminary support for the reliability of these assessments with autistic adolescents.

Importantly, a common interview of adolescent depression (K-SADS) showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across autistic adolescents and their parents, providing initial support for the use of this interview to assess the presence (and severity) of depression in autistic adolescents.

Confirmatory factor analyses demonstrated that adolescent-reported anhedonia on the ASA was the only model with a good fit across indices (i.e., without disagreement) whereas other models showed mixed or poor fit, which may reflect model misspecification, the modest sample size, or limited prior psychometric data.

In terms of validity, all three SMI subscales correlated positively with the ACIPS and the KSADS-Depression correlated with RCADS-Depression, as hypothesized, while the LARS-ASA convergent pair showed a smaller positive correlation than the other convergent pairs.

Agreement between adolescent self-report and parent report ranged widely with most assessments falling in the poor-to-moderate range; findings align with previous research on neurotypical adolescent/parent disagreement on internalizing and motivation-related constructs.

Confirmatory factor analyses showed good fit for the ASA and adolescent-report KSADS-Depression, mixed fit for the ACIPS and RCADS-Depression, and poor fit for the SMI, LARS, and parent-report KSADS-Depression.
The ASA's perfect CFI/TLI (1.00) may reflect few degrees of freedom and warrants replication.

Overall, the findings provide preliminary support for the ASA, RCADS-Depression, and adolescent-report KSADS-Depression; tentative support for the ACIPS; and a basis for caution with the SMI, LARS total score, and parent-report KSADS-Depression.
These results support use of the better-supported measures in current and future mental health research with autistic adolescents and their families, with further validation needed for the others.
Our findings align with some previous research supporting the use of generic mental health assessments with autistic adolescents 18 .

text.text: However, the extent to which autism-specific adaptations to these assessments may enhance internal consistency and other psychometric properties remains untested.

As noted, internal consistency results for the parent-report KSADS were lower than other assessments and may be attributed to the internalizing nature of depressive symptoms that might not be readily observed by parents.
It is also possible that alexithymia or other social communication differences common among autistic adolescents 12 prevent full disclosure of their internalizing states to parents.

text.text: Though the LARS reliability overall was acceptable, a closer investigation shows that most of that reliability is derived from the nine separate sub-domains and not from one unified "apathy" factor.

Thus, the LARS total score may not provide meaningful information on its own (i.e., one coherent apathy measure) for autistic adolescents and their parents and instead, the nine sub-domains may provide more useful information.
In terms of convergent/discriminant validity, findings suggest modest convergent validity between measures of similar constructs.
Among adolescent self-reports, hypothesized convergent pairs correlated more strongly than cross-construct pairs, which is the basic pattern expected, though the gap was modest.
The SMI and ACIPS behaved as expected, with all SMI subscales correlating positively with the ACIPS-Total, and the two depression measures (KSADS and RCADS) showed a moderate-to-strong association.
One notable exception was the LARS-ASA pair, which we expected to overlap given the conceptual relationship between apathy and anhedonia but correlated only weakly.
This may suggest that the LARS does not map neatly onto adolescent anhedonia as captured by the ASA, though this interpretation is tentative.
Notably, the LARS-Total correlated more strongly with the ACIPS-Total, indicating that apathy overlaps substantially with reduced pleasure.
The ASA also correlated highly with both depression measures.
Finally, the parent-report validity evidence is limited, as only one convergent pair could be evaluated as the ACIPS and ASA have no parent versions.
Although this correlation exceeded the mean of the discriminant pairs, it rests on a single comparison and should be interpreted cautiously.
Cross-informant agreement between adolescents and their parents ranged from poor to moderate for all assessments, with the strongest agreement observed for adolescent social behaviors on the SMI.

Findings align with previous work showcasing significant cross-informant disagreement between neurotypical adolescents and their parents 31 as well as autistic youth and their parents. 27 In our study, adolescents reported stronger skills than those reported by their parents in the areas of social success (SMI) and emotional reactivity (LARS), yet adolescents endorsed a higher severity of depressive symptoms.

text.text: It is possible that adolescents' perceived success in social situations with peers, internal emotional states, and internalizing depressive symptoms may not be readily observable to parents, contributing to discrepant ratings.

Of note, depression scores were discrepant across raters when assessed by a questionnaire (RCADS) with adolescents endorsing more severe symptoms than those reported by their parents, yet depression severity was not significantly different across raters on an interview (K-SADS).

It is possible that adolescents disclose more of their distress on questionnaires as this assessment method lacks the social exchange of an interview, which may be experienced as stressful. 18, 22 These findings are consistent with previous work suggesting that self-report questionnaires paired with interviews may better detect autistic youth at risk for mental health distress. 18 Clinically, findings emphasize the importance of understanding both adolescent and parent perspectives in detecting and addressing mental health distress in autistic adolescents.

text.text: The present study was among the first to assess the psychometric properties of several interviews and questionnaires of mental health outcomes and risk/protective factors in a moderate sample of autistic adolescents and their parents, with findings that can guide future research in this area.
At the same time, there are several limitations to the present study that warrant discussion.

First, the sample size was modest, which limited our ability to robustly test multi-factor models; the confirmatory factor analyses for the LARS and SMI in particular should be interpreted cautiously, as fit indices may be unstable.
Second, though missing data is common in clinical research, it limited our ability to include assessments from all participants.
Third, assessments were administered at a single timepoint, so we could not evaluate test-retest reliability, and we did not assess inter-rater reliability for the KSADS.
Fourth, tests of convergent validity were limited for some measures (e.g., the LARS had a single hypothesized comparator, the ASA).
This study provides preliminary evidence on the psychometric properties of several mental health measures in autistic adolescents and their parents.

Most measures showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across informants, while confirmatory factor analyses yielded mixed evidence of structural validity, with only the ASA showing good fit across all indices.

Convergent validity was moderate: related measures generally correlated more strongly than unrelated ones, though the LARS showed weaker-than-expected overlap with the ASA, and its reliability appeared to depend largely on its nine domain-level factors rather than a single general apathy factor.
Adolescent and parent reports agreed poorly to moderately, which emphasizes the value of collecting both perspectives.

Taken together, these findings support the continued use of several of these measures in autistic adolescents, particularly the ASA, ACIPS, KSADS adolescent report, and RCADS, while suggesting caution in interpreting the LARS total score and SMI structure.

Replication in larger samples, with longitudinal designs and autism-specific adaptations, is needed to confirm these findings and clarify how well these measures capture mental health in autistic youth.
